summary: There's a big new result -- in fact, pair of results -- on arXiv this morning, due to James Leng, Ashwin Sah and Mehtaab Sawhney. One of them beats a record that I had been quite pleased to hold for the last quarter of a century (though I'm also happy it's been broken). 🧵

title: Timothy Gowers @wtgowers (@wtgowers)
summary: The record concerns a famous theorem of Szemerédi, which asserts that for every positive real number c and every positive integer k, there is some n such that if A is any subset of {1,2,...,n} of size at least cn, then A must contain an arithmetic progression of length k. 2/7

title: Timothy Gowers @wtgowers (@wtgowers)
summary: That leaves open the question of how large n needs to be. I showed in 1998 that it is enough if n is greater than 2^2^(1/c)^2^2^{k+9} (where a^b^c means a^(b^c)). For k > 5 this had not been improved until today. (The record for k=5 was broken recently by the same authors.) 3/7

title: Timothy Gowers @wtgowers (@wtgowers)
summary: Here's the paper that establishes the new bound. They get a bound of 2^2^(log(1/c))^C, where C is some constant that depends on k only. For small c, this is a big improvement -- replacing the (1/c) I got by log(1/c). 4/7

title: Timothy Gowers @wtgowers (@wtgowers)
summary:
It did this by solving four of the six problems completely, which got it 28 points out of a possible total of 42. I'm not quite sure, but I think that put it ahead of all but around 60 competitors.
However, that statement needs a bit of qualifying.

title: Timothy Gowers @wtgowers (@wtgowers)
summary: The main qualification is that the program needed a lot longer than the human competitors -- for some of the problems over 60 hours -- and of course much faster processing speed than the poor old human brain.

title: Timothy Gowers @wtgowers (@wtgowers)
summary:
If the human competitors had been allowed that sort of time per problem they would undoubtedly have scored higher.
Nevertheless, (i) this is well beyond what automatic theorem provers could do before, and (ii) these times are likely to come down as efficiency gains are made.

title: Timothy Gowers @wtgowers (@wtgowers)
summary: Another qualification is that the problems were manually translated into the proof assistant Lean, and only then did the program get to work. But the essential mathematics was done by the program: just the autoformalization part was done by humans.

title: Timothy Gowers @wtgowers (@wtgowers)
summary: As with AlphaGo, the program learnt to do what it did by teaching itself. But for that it needed a big collection of problems to work on. They achieved that in an interesting way: they took a huge database of IMO-type problems and got a large language model to formalize them.

title: Timothy Gowers @wtgowers (@wtgowers)
summary: However, LLMs are not able to autoformalize reliably, so they got them to autoformalize each problem many times. Some of the formalizations were correct, but even the incorrect ones were useful as training data, as often they were easier problems.

title: Timothy Gowers @wtgowers (@wtgowers)
summary: So we might be close to having a program that would enable mathematicians to get answers to a wide range of questions, provided those questions weren't *too* difficult -- the kind of thing one can do in a couple of hours.

clean_title: Major breakthrough in additive combinatorics disproves the sum-product conjecture over the reals
summary:
Another major problem, this time in additive combinatorics, has fallen, this time to humans rather than AI, but using methods related to the AI solution to the unit distance conjecture.
Quoting @mehtaab_sawhney
A remarkable paper appeared on arXiv tonight by Thomas Bloom, Will Sawin, Carl Schildkraut and Dmitrii Zhelezov. In this paper, they prove that there exists c>0 and arbitrarily large finite sets A of real numbers such that max(|A+A|,|AA|)≤|A|^{2-c}. This disproves the well-known sum-product conjecture over the real numbers. The sum-product conjecture considers the two most basic operations: addition and multiplication. A+A is the set of all pairwise sums of two elements in A while AA is the set of all pairwise products of two elements in A. (1/5)
clean_summary: Another major problem in additive combinatorics has been solved by humans using methods related to those in AI research, rather than by AI itself. A remarkable paper by Bloom, Sawin, Schildkraut, and Zhelezov proves that there exist large finite sets of real numbers A where the maximum of the sizes of A+A and AA is significantly smaller than previously thought, specifically at most |A|^{2-c} for some c>0. This result disproves the well-known sum-product conjecture over the real numbers, which posited that the sum set and product set of A cannot both be small simultaneously, considering the basic operations of addition and multiplication.
